title: Secure a free-standing gas cylinder to its wall bracket with the bracket's chain
instruction: Secure the gas cylinder to the wall bracket with the bracket's chain so that it cannot tip over. Keep the cylinder upright the whole time, do not touch its valve, and finish with both grippers away from the cylinder and the chain.
context: Securing a gas cylinder upright to a wall bracket is routine for welders, cutters, solderers and brazers (SOC 51-4121, about 457,300 US jobs in 2024, BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook), plumbers, pipefitters and steamfitters (47-2152, about 504,500; brazing and purge gas), HVAC mechanics and installers (49-9021, about 440,900 in 2025; nitrogen, refrigerant and oxy-acetylene cylinders), plus lab technicians, respiratory therapists and gas-delivery drivers: well over a million workers together. Every cylinder that is set down, changed or delivered must be restrained upright (OSHA 29 CFR 1926.350(a)(9), NFPA 55, CGA P-1); a knocked-over cylinder can shear its valve. The usual way (not given to the robot): steady the cylinder in the bracket's cradle, take the chain round its front at chain height (above its centre of gravity, below the shoulder) and drop the link nearest the J-hook onto it so the chain holds the cylinder back against the bracket, without knocking the valve.
setup: Positions are measured forward from the line joining the two arm bases (61 cm apart), left or right of their midline as seen from behind the robot, and up from the table top. Both arms start at the ready pose with grippers open. One fixed layout, as in the screenshot. Wall: an 18 mm plywood panel standing on the table across the back, its front face 43 cm in front of the bases, 50 cm wide (20 cm left to 30 cm right of the midline), 50 cm tall, fixed. Bracket: a Bristol Maid CYB/DE2 grey steel wall bracket for two D/E cylinders (359 x 107 x 88 mm): an 88 mm wall flange screwed to the panel and a 3 mm plate sticking out 107 mm, its top 33 cm above the table, spanning 8.9 cm left to 27.1 cm right of the midline, with two U-shaped cradles 117 mm wide edged with black bumper strip; the left cradle is centred on the midline, the right one 18.2 cm right of it is empty. The cylinder's chain is fixed through a hole in the tongue between the cradles, 33.3 cm in front of the bases and 8.1 cm right of the midline; on the other side, under the plate's left end, hangs a J-hook of 6 mm round bar: stem 32.9 cm in front of the bases and 7.6 cm left of the midline, 50 mm long, its bend opening forward and its tip rising 22 mm, 31.3 cm in front of the bases (just in front of the plate's edge), top 30.2 cm above the table. Chain: zinc-plated welded long-link chain, 13 links of 4 mm wire, 28 x 11 mm inside (7 g each), hanging from its hole to the table, the last link and a half lying on the table toward the robot; the end link has a red PVC sleeve, about 28.5 cm in front of the bases and 8 cm right of the midline. Cylinder: an aluminium size MD medical oxygen cylinder (111 mm diameter, straight wall to 37 cm, shoulder painted green, neck top 42.4 cm; CGA 870 brass post valve 32 x 30 x 45 mm on top with a black toggle standing up to 49.9 cm; 3.3 kg, centre of gravity 20 cm up), standing loose and upright on the table in the left cradle, its axis on the midline 35.9 cm in front of the bases, 1 mm in front of the cradle's back.
scoring: Score 0 if, at any time before the after-release check, the cylinder tilts more than 10 degrees from upright, or its valve or toggle is knocked (a finger comes within 15 mm of them, or the chain within 8 mm). Otherwise the score is the highest level reached: 0.25 if the chain crosses the cylinder's front against it (within 3 cm of its surface where it crosses the middle of the front) anywhere up its straight wall; 0.5 if also the chain sits in the J-hook (a link down in its bend, between the stem and the upturned tip) for at least 0.5 s; 0.75 if, with the chain hooked, it crosses the cylinder's front between 25 and 36 cm above the table (the upper third of the straight wall, below the shoulder), it is snug (the hooked link is at most 30 mm further along the chain than the 290 mm the chain takes when pulled tight round this cylinder: the eleventh link from the hole, or none further), and the cylinder is upright within 3 degrees with less than 6 mm between it and the cradle's back; 1.0 if the after-release check also passes. After-release check, done once the chain is hooked and every finger has stayed at least 5 cm from the cylinder and the chain for 1 s without a break (the count restarts if one comes closer): pull the cylinder at 40 cm up (just under the neck) horizontally toward the robot with 10 N for 2 s (a loose cylinder tips at about 4 N); pass if it tilts less than 6 degrees and the 0.75 conditions held when the check started. Tilt from an inclinometer on the shoulder; heights and gaps with a rule and feeler; the hooked link by counting links from the hole.
reset_notes: Lift the chain out of the J-hook and let it hang from its hole with the last link and a half lying on the table toward the robot, red sleeve up. Stand the cylinder upright back in the left cradle against its back, valve toggle closed and pointing up; if it fell, check the valve before reuse (an empty or practice cylinder is advised). About 1 minute.
fidelity: PhysX at 480 Hz, arms with the station's i2rt gains. Free rigid cylinder; chain = 13 rigid long links whose wire rings collide, on alternating hinges, so the J-hook holds a link by shape alone (the bracket has no gate). Bracket cradle, hook and chain sizes read from the data-sheet photos; snug = hooked link's count from the hole; red sleeve ours; check force applied in sim. Details in README.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (never reaches the chain); demo (cameras and joint states only): 1.0; control (end brought two links short so no link seats in the hook, forced after-release check): 0.25
